title: Advance Market Commitments for Vaccines
description: 2004. Pharmaceutical companies won't develop vaccines for diseases affecting only the poor. The market fails because customers can't pay. Can you design a mechanism to make unprofitable vaccines profitable—and save millions of lives?

decisions.title: The Market Failure
decisions.contextCard: Pneumococcal disease kills 1 million children annually, mostly in poor countries. Vaccines exist for rich-world strains but not for those prevalent in Africa and Asia. R&D costs $300-700 million. No company will invest because the poor can't pay. Traditional aid is unpredictable. You need a new mechanism.

choices.text: Develop theoretical framework—show how advance commitments solve the credible payment problem
Study pharmaceutical industry incentives—understand exactly what would make vaccine development profitable
Build coalition with global health advocates—GAVI, WHO, Gates Foundation, MSF

decisions.title: Designing the Commitment
decisions.contextCard: You're designing an Advance Market Commitment (AMC). Donors pre-commit to buy vaccines at a guaranteed price if developed. Key parameters: commitment size, price per dose, eligibility criteria, purchase obligations. Too generous wastes donor money. Too stingy won't incentivize development. Lives depend on getting this right.

choices.text: Propose $1.5 billion commitment for pneumococcal vaccine—enough to justify R&D, credible for pharma
Design tail price mechanism—subsidized initial doses, then lower 'tail' price for long-term supply

decisions.title: Building Donor Support
decisions.contextCard: You need $1.5 billion in donor commitments. This isn't traditional aid—it's a market mechanism. Some donors are skeptical: 'Why guarantee pharma profits?' Others worry about precedent. The framing matters—is this corporate welfare or innovative development finance?

choices.text: Frame as smart aid—pays only for results, creates sustainable supply, saves more lives per dollar
Emphasize risk-sharing—donors and pharma both commit resources, neither bears all risk alone

decisions.title: Launch and Wait
decisions.contextCard: February 2007: Italy, UK, Canada, Russia, Norway, and Gates Foundation commit $1.5 billion for pneumococcal AMC. Now the wait begins. Will pharmaceutical companies respond? Will they actually develop and test vaccines for developing-world strains? This could take years. Patience and credibility are crucial.

choices.text: Maintain donor coalition—ensure commitments remain credible despite political changes
Engage pharmaceutical companies—provide technical support, reduce regulatory uncertainty
Build developing country capacity—ensure health systems ready to deliver vaccines when available

decisions.title: The Vaccines Arrive
decisions.contextCard: It works! Pfizer and GlaxoSmithKline develop pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCV) covering developing-world strains. Trials show 90%+ efficacy. WHO pre-qualifies them. GAVI begins procurement through the AMC. The mechanism that was once theoretical is now saving real children's lives.

choices.text: Document success rigorously—show how AMC incentivized R&D that wouldn't have occurred otherwise
Optimize rollout—work with countries to maximize vaccination coverage and impact
Advocate for AMC expansion—malaria, tuberculosis, other neglected diseases need similar mechanisms

decisions.title: Scaling Impact
decisions.contextCard: The pneumococcal AMC has delivered over 150 million vaccine doses to 60+ countries. Pneumococcal disease deaths are dropping dramatically. But challenges remain: supply constraints, vaccine hesitancy, cold chain logistics, and questions about long-term sustainability beyond the AMC.

choices.text: Research impact rigorously—estimate lives saved, cost-effectiveness, compare to counterfactual
Address supply bottlenecks—support new manufacturers, technology transfer, competition
Plan for sustainability—ensure vaccine supply continues after initial AMC commitment expires

decisions.title: The COVID Test
decisions.contextCard: COVID-19 emerges. The world needs vaccines urgently. Operation Warp Speed and COVAX both use AMC-inspired mechanisms—advance purchase commitments guarantee pharma revenue, incentivizing unprecedented R&D speed. Your decade-old idea is now being deployed at global scale, under unimaginable pressure.

choices.text: Advise COVID vaccine initiatives—apply lessons from pneumococcal AMC to emergency context
Advocate for equitable access—ensure COVAX reaches developing countries, not just rich nations
Document COVID as AMC validation—show how advance commitments accelerated unprecedented innovation

decisions.title: Proven Mechanism
decisions.contextCard: The pneumococcal AMC has saved an estimated 700,000+ lives. COVID vaccines reached billions in record time, partly due to AMC-style mechanisms. The concept has proven itself at both endemic and pandemic scales. Market design can solve problems traditional aid cannot. The mechanism works.

choices.text: Expand to other diseases—advocate for AMCs for tuberculosis, malaria, neglected tropical diseases
Apply AMC concept to climate—advance commitments for green technologies, carbon removal, adaptation
Train next generation—teach market design for social impact to economists and policymakers worldwide
